← Border Closure Atlas

Evidence review · 25 October 2026

What happened after the last report?

All 221 records with ambiguous later status have been reviewed. A later reopening, policy change or access report can bound an old restriction without proving that the border is open today. Current restrictions are separately dated and retain their exceptions.

221records reviewed · 250 phases
106records with adopted map updates
118records retaining an unresolved phase

The last two groups overlap where only some phases could be resolved. 122 phase markers were updated; 128 phases remain unverified. The map includes 33 status records with 45 separately dated periods. Effective dates and later checks are distinct.

The COVID follow-up added 21 phase updates across 19 records, including 18 newly integrated records. Each corrected phase marker ends at its own supported date across the timeline; unmatched phases retain their uncertainty.

The chronology follow-up checks all 33 status observations. Ukraine’s Russia and Belarus closure starts on 28 February 2022; six standing regimes predate October 2016. Rafah reopenings, later reclosures and changes of scope are separate phases.

How to interpret this review

Record-by-record searches for later reopening, continuing restriction and current guidance; government, border agency, customs, UN and direct operational reporting preferred. Scope checked by crossing, movement, direction, cohort and commodity. Plans, expired orders, fresh crawl dates, opposite-direction movement and unrelated ports were not treated as reopenings. Sources shown include both adopted evidence and rejected or insufficient leads as explained in each finding. Search-result extracts were used where direct retrieval failed; this is a source review, not field verification or independent human review.

All 221 records (250 last-confirmed phases) in the endpoint review inventory were researched on 25 October 2026. Findings distinguish current restrictions, later access bounds, changed scope, partial evidence, conflicting evidence and unresolved status. Selected map updates received source-text, date and scope checks; unavailable full text and inadequate evidence remain qualified. Standing official guidance is dated to the check; news observations retain their event/report date. A later access bound suppresses only the matching old unknown marker from that bound onward. It does not label the border open, alter historical durations, fill gaps or merge later reclosures. Status verification dates are not closure starts. Separately reviewed timeline periods show a restriction from its sourced effective date through its latest supporting evidence, with changing scopes, exceptions and reopenings separated. Pre-window regimes are labelled as already in force, not newly starting at the window boundary. Unreviewed snapshots, if any, remain confined to their evidence month. These supplemental periods are excluded from episode and duration statistics. Coverage concerns this fixed inventory, not every world frontier. A further COVID-focused pass separates the ending of a national prohibition from reopening every individual port. Each new resolution records whether it is based on policy cessation or later access; neither establishes present-day openness.

“End supported by later evidence” means the recorded restriction had ended by a supported later date. For a national policy, this can establish the end of the prohibition without proving that every individual port reopened. It is not an exact reopening date or a claim of unrestricted access now. “Restriction confirmed” uses current official guidance or recent reporting; operator reports are separately labelled. Changed scope, partial, historical and conflicting evidence are not converted into a whole-border conclusion.

Historical dates, durations and episode totals are preserved. Observations checked after the original 21 October 2026 study cutoff display their actual dates. No verified crossing position means no map position is invented.

North–South Korea: ordinary cross-border travel unavailable

  • Already in force before October 2016 · confirmed through 2026-10-15

    Standing restriction on whole inter-korean boundary for ordinary civilian travel. Authorised exceptions remain separate.

    Whole inter-Korean boundary for ordinary civilian travel

The 1953 armistice requires specific authorisation for crossings of the Military Demarcation Line. The UN Command continues to administer that regime and current Canadian advice confirms ordinary travel between the Koreas is unavailable. Authorised industrial, humanitarian, diplomatic and organised visits are exceptions; this is not a claim of zero crossings since 1953.
